subject: rla
title: Word Meaning, Tone, and Figurative Language
objectives: Students will use context clues (definition, example, contrast, and cause and effect) to determine the meaning of unfamiliar and multiple-meaning words as they are used in a text.
Students will distinguish denotation from connotation and explain how an author's word choice creates a positive, negative, or neutral feeling.
Students will identify the tone of a text (the author's or narrator's attitude) and the mood (the feeling created in the reader) and cite the words that create each.
Students will identify similes, metaphors, personification, and idioms in literary texts and explain what each one means and why the author used it.
Students will answer GED-style word meaning, tone, and figurative language questions, including dropdown word-choice items and click-the-sentence items.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 4 moves learners into literary reading: stories and personal narratives. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA) test, literary passages make up about a quarter of the reading, and they are full of questions about words: what a word means in this sentence, what feeling a word carries, what a comparison suggests, and what attitude or atmosphere the writer creates. These questions reward careful readers more than readers with big vocabularies. Tell learners early: you do not need to know every word. You need to know how to use the sentence around it.

Objectives

  • Use context clues to find the meaning of a word as it is used in a sentence.
  • Explain the difference between denotation and connotation.
  • Tell tone from mood and name the words that create each.
  • Identify and interpret similes, metaphors, personification, and idioms.
  • Answer GED-style word meaning, tone, and figurative language questions.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; highlighters in two colors (one for positive words, one for negative words)
  • The warm-up word pairs, the four worked examples, and the guided-practice passage below
  • Week 4 practice items (items 1–8 use the story “Last Call at the Blue Kettle” and are used for independent practice)
  • Index cards or a shared document for the exit ticket

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Same meaning, different feeling”: sort word pairs as positive or negative
Direct instruction20Context clues; denotation and connotation; tone vs. mood; simile, metaphor, personification, idiom; four worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group reading of “The Waiting Room,” five questions
Independent practice15Practice items 1–8 (Blue Kettle story); circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Same meaning, different feeling

Write these pairs on the board. Each pair has nearly the same dictionary meaning. Learners mark which word in each pair sounds positive and which sounds negative.

thrifty / cheap    curious / nosy    confident / arrogant    aroma / stench    determined / stubborn    slim / scrawny

Answers: Positive: thrifty, curious, confident, aroma, determined, slim. Negative: cheap, nosy, arrogant, stench, stubborn, scrawny. Then ask: “If I call you thrifty, am I complimenting you? If I call you cheap?” Expected: thrifty is a compliment (careful with money); cheap is an insult (unwilling to spend). Say: “Same basic meaning, very different feeling. That feeling is called connotation, and writers choose words for it on purpose.”

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: Word meaning in context (5 minutes)

Say: “GED questions ask what a word means as it is used in the passage. That phrase is a warning. The answer is often not the first dictionary meaning.” Teach four kinds of context clues:

  • Definition or restatement: the sentence explains the word. (He was frugal; he never spent a dollar he did not have to.)
  • Example: the sentence gives examples. (Root vegetables, such as carrots, beets, and turnips, keep well in winter.)
  • Contrast: a word like but, although, or unlike signals the opposite. (Unlike her talkative sister, Rosa was reticent.)
  • Cause and effect: the result explains the word. (The trail was so treacherous that two hikers turned back.)

Then teach the replacement test: cover the word, put each answer choice in its place, and reread the sentence. The right choice keeps the sentence's meaning. Stress multiple-meaning words such as modest, bright, run, and cold: learners must test each meaning against the sentence.

Talking point 2: Denotation and connotation (3 minutes)

Connect back to the warm-up. Denotation is the dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling or association a word carries: positive, negative, or neutral. Ask: “Why would a writer call a house cozy instead of cramped?” Expected: to make the reader feel warmth instead of discomfort. On the GED, questions such as “Why does the author use the word ___?” are connotation questions.

Talking point 3: Tone vs. mood (4 minutes)

Draw two arrows on the board. One arrow points from the writer to the subject: that is tone, the writer's or narrator's attitude (amused, bitter, admiring, sarcastic, nostalgic). The other arrow points from the text to the reader: that is mood, the atmosphere or feeling the reader gets (tense, peaceful, gloomy, hopeful). Tell learners to find tone and mood the same way: highlight the strongest words, sort them as positive or negative, then choose a precise word. Warn them that extreme choices (furious, ecstatic, terrified) are usually wrong unless the text is extreme too.

Talking point 4: Figurative language (6 minutes)

Literal language means exactly what it says. Figurative language means more than, or something different from, what it says. Build this table with the class:

TypeWhat it doesExample
SimileCompares two unlike things using like or asThe hallway was as quiet as a library.
MetaphorCompares by saying one thing is another, without like or asThe hallway was a tomb.
PersonificationGives human actions or feelings to something not humanThe old furnace groaned all night.
IdiomA common expression whose meaning cannot be figured out word by wordShe was on the fence about the job. (undecided)
HyperboleDeliberate exaggerationI have told you a million times.

Teach a three-step routine for any figure of speech: (1) Name it (which type?). (2) Unpack it: what two things are compared, and what quality do they share? (3) Explain the effect: what does it make the reader see or feel?

Talking point 5: How these questions are worded (2 minutes)

Show the stems learners will see: “As used in paragraph 3, the word ___ most nearly means…”, “What does the phrase ___ suggest about the character?”, “Which word best describes the mood of the paragraph?”, “The author's use of ___ helps to…”. Point out that suggest and helps to ask about effect, not just definition.

Worked examples

Example 1: A multiple-meaning word in context

“After the plant closed, Ray took a job at the hardware store. The pay was modest, but the hours were steady, and he liked being able to tell his kids he would be home for dinner.”

Question: As used in the passage, modest most nearly means (a) humble about one's achievements, (b) small or limited, (c) shy, (d) polite.

Solution. Step 1: Find the clue. The word but sets up a contrast: the pay is a drawback, and the steady hours are a benefit. Step 2: So modest must describe something not very good about the pay. Step 3: Replacement test: “The pay was small, but the hours were steady” makes sense. “The pay was humble about its achievements” does not. Answer: (b). Choices (a), (c), and (d) are real meanings of modest or near-synonyms, but they describe people, not paychecks. This is the classic trap: a correct definition in the wrong context.

Example 2: Tone from word choice

“Our new manager, Mr. Pratt, loves rules. He has rules about lunch breaks, rules about stacking boxes, and, I am not making this up, a rule about how loudly we may sneeze. Last week he sent a two-page memo about pens.”

Question: Which word best describes the narrator's tone? (a) admiring, (b) amused, (c) furious, (d) frightened.

Solution. Step 1: Highlight the strongest words and details: “loves rules,” the repeated “rules about,” “I am not making this up,” “a rule about how loudly we may sneeze,” “a two-page memo about pens.” Step 2: Sort them. The narrator is poking fun; the details are chosen because they sound silly. Step 3: Choose the precise word: (b) amused (a mocking, joking attitude). Choice (a) is the opposite. Choice (c) is too extreme; nothing shows real anger. Choice (d) has no support at all.

Example 3: Unpacking a metaphor

“After my brother left for the Army, hope was a candle my mother kept burning in the front window. Neighbors stopped asking about him after the first year. She never stopped setting his place at the table.”

Question: What does the metaphor in the first sentence suggest about the mother?

Solution. Step 1, name it: “hope was a candle” is a metaphor (no like or as). Step 2, unpack it: hope is compared to a candle. A candle is small but steady, it must be tended to stay lit, and a candle in a window is a signal for someone to come home. Step 3, effect: the mother keeps hoping, quietly and faithfully, for her son's return, even when others have given up. The last two sentences confirm this: neighbors stopped asking, but she kept setting his place.

Example 4: Reading an idiom

“When Tasha learned the concert was sold out, she shrugged and said, ‘That's the way the cookie crumbles.’ Then she bought tickets for next month's show.”

Question: What does Tasha's comment show about her?

Solution. Step 1: Read literally, the sentence is about a cookie, which makes no sense here, so it is an idiom. Step 2: The idiom means “things do not always go your way, and you have to accept it.” Step 3: Check the context: she shrugged and made a new plan right away. The idiom shows that Tasha accepts disappointment calmly and moves on. A learner who answers “she was upset about food” read the idiom literally.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Read this passage aloud twice. On the second reading, learners highlight every figure of speech and every word that creates feeling. Then work through the questions together, asking learners to point to evidence before you confirm an answer.

The Waiting Room

The emergency waiting room was a fishbowl of fluorescent light. Andre had been sitting in the same plastic chair for three hours, and the clock above the nurses' station seemed to be dragging its hands on purpose. Every time the double doors swung open, his heart leapt into his throat. A vending machine hummed in the corner, the only thing in the room that sounded calm. Then a nurse in green scrubs walked toward him, smiling, and for the first time all night, Andre let out the breath he had been holding.

  1. What type of figurative language is “a fishbowl of fluorescent light,” and what does it suggest? Answer: Metaphor. Like a fish in a bowl, Andre feels closed in, exposed, and on display under harsh, artificial light.
  2. What does “the clock…seemed to be dragging its hands on purpose” suggest? Answer: Personification. Time feels painfully slow to Andre, almost as if the clock is being cruel to him.
  3. What does “his heart leapt into his throat” mean? Answer: It is an idiom (and an exaggeration) meaning he felt a sudden jolt of fear or anxiety.
  4. Which word best describes the mood of the first four sentences: peaceful, tense, or cheerful? Answer: Tense. Evidence: three hours in the same chair, the slow clock, his heart leaping each time the doors open. Even the “calm” vending machine highlights that nothing else is calm.
  5. How does the last sentence change the mood? Answer: It shifts from tension to relief. The smiling nurse and the released breath signal good news.

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–8, all based on the story “Last Call at the Blue Kettle.” Circulate. When a learner is stuck, ask the three routine questions: “What type is it? What is being compared? What does it make you see or feel?” For word-meaning items, ask them to say the replacement sentence aloud. Learners who finish early can start items 9–11 (the swimming narrative).

Checks for understanding

  • “What is the difference between tone and mood?” Expected: Tone is the writer's or narrator's attitude; mood is the feeling the reader gets.
  • “Is ‘The snow was a white blanket’ a simile or a metaphor? How do you know?” Expected: Metaphor, because it says the snow was a blanket, with no like or as.
  • “What does ‘break the ice’ mean in ‘Rosa told a joke to break the ice at the meeting’?” Expected: To ease tension and get people talking at the start of something.
  • “Give a word with a more positive connotation than stubborn.” Expected: determined, persistent, or firm.
  • “What should you do after you pick an answer to a word-in-context question?” Expected: Put it into the sentence and reread to make sure the meaning still works.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Choosing the dictionary meaning, not the context meaning. Learners see a familiar word and pick its most common meaning. Correction: Require the replacement test on every word-meaning item. Ask, “Does your choice make sense in this sentence?”

Mixing up tone and mood. A narrator can sound calm (tone) while the reader feels dread (mood). Correction: Use the two-arrow drawing. Ask, “Is the question about the writer's attitude or the reader's feeling?”

Reading idioms literally. “By heart” has nothing to do with the heart. Correction: If the literal meaning makes no sense in the context, treat the phrase as an idiom and use the surrounding sentences to decide what it means.

Calling every comparison a metaphor. Correction: Look for like or as first. If it is there and two unlike things are compared, it is a simile.

Picking extreme tone words. Correction: Ask, “Could I point to a word that is that strong?” If not, choose the milder, more precise answer.

Differentiation

Support: Give learners a tone-and-mood word bank sorted into positive, negative, and neutral columns. Let them work the guided-practice passage in pairs, one reading aloud and one highlighting. For figurative language, start with just simile vs. metaphor before adding personification and idioms. Provide sentence frames: “The author compares ___ to ___ to show that ___.”

Stretch: Ask learners to rewrite a neutral sentence twice, once with positive and once with negative connotation (“The man walked into the room” becomes “strolled” or “stomped”). Have them explain how a single figure of speech in the Blue Kettle story contributes to the theme of the whole story, and write one original simile and one original metaphor about their own neighborhood.

How this shows up on the GED

On the RLA test, expect several questions per literary passage on word meaning and language. Common formats:

  • Multiple choice: “As used in paragraph 4, the word ___ most nearly means…” and “What does the phrase ___ suggest about ___?”
  • Tone and mood: “Which word best describes the narrator's attitude toward ___?” or “How does the author create a sense of ___ in paragraph 2?”
  • Effect of word choice: “The author uses the word ___ rather than ___ in order to…”
  • Dropdown editing: in a draft letter or article, choose the word or phrase that fits the meaning and tone (for example, a respectful word in a tribute, or the correct idiom).
  • Click the sentence (hotspot): “Click the sentence that contains personification” or “that best shows the narrator's change in attitude.”

Remind learners that this week's Practice GED includes literary passages, so the routines from this lesson will pay off there directly.
student:
Why this skill matters

On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will read stories and personal narratives, and many questions will ask about the words the writer chose. What does this word mean here? Why did the author pick it? What feeling does this paragraph create? What does this comparison suggest? The good news: you do not need a huge vocabulary. You need a few reliable methods, and you will learn them this week.

Finding word meaning from context

When a question says “as used in the passage,” it is asking for the meaning in that sentence, which may not be the most common meaning. Look for these clues:

Clue typeWhat to look forExample
Definition or restatementThe sentence explains the word, often after a comma, dash, or semicolonMarcus was frugal; he never spent a dollar he did not need to.
Examplesuch as, for example, includingShe loved citrus fruits such as lemons, limes, and oranges.
Contrastbut, although, unlike, howeverUnlike his chatty brother, Leo was reticent. (quiet, reserved)
Cause and effectso, because, as a resultThe ice made the road so treacherous that the school closed. (dangerous)

The replacement test: Cover the word. Put each answer choice in its place. Reread the sentence. The correct answer keeps the meaning and makes sense.

Denotation and connotation

The denotation of a word is its dictionary meaning. The connotation is the feeling the word carries. Slim and scrawny both mean thin, but slim sounds attractive and scrawny sounds weak. Determined and stubborn both mean someone will not give up, but one is praise and one is a complaint. Writers choose words for their connotations, so when a question asks why the author used a certain word, think about the feeling, not just the definition.

Tone and mood

ToneMood
What it isThe writer's or narrator's attitude toward the subjectThe feeling or atmosphere the reader experiences
Ask yourselfHow does the writer feel about this?How does this make me feel?
Example wordsadmiring, amused, bitter, sarcastic, nostalgic, respectfultense, peaceful, gloomy, hopeful, eerie, joyful

To find tone or mood: (1) highlight the strongest words and details; (2) decide whether they are mostly positive or negative; (3) pick the most precise word. Avoid extreme answers unless the text is extreme.

Figurative language

Literal language means exactly what it says. Figurative language means something more. Learn these four types:

  • Simile: compares two unlike things using like or as. “The parking lot was as empty as a ghost town.”
  • Metaphor: compares by saying one thing is another. “The parking lot was a desert.”
  • Personification: gives human actions or feelings to something not human. “The wind whispered through the trees.”
  • Idiom: a common saying whose meaning is different from its words. “It's raining cats and dogs” means it is raining very hard.

Three steps for any figure of speech: (1) Name it. (2) Unpack it: what is being compared, and what do the two things have in common? (3) Explain the effect: what does it help you see or feel?

Worked examples

Example 1: Context clues. “The forecast called for a deluge, so Mia moved the party indoors. Sure enough, by noon the rain was pouring so hard that the gutters overflowed.” What does deluge mean?

Step 1: Look for clues. Mia moved the party indoors, and the rain made the gutters overflow. Step 2: Those clues point to a lot of rain. Step 3: Replace: “The forecast called for very heavy rain.” It works. Answer: a deluge is a very heavy rainfall or flood.

Example 2: Connotation. A news story says a mayor's plan is “bold.” Another says it is “reckless.” What is the difference?

Step 1: Both words describe a plan that takes risks (the denotation). Step 2: Bold is positive: brave and confident. Reckless is negative: careless about danger. Answer: the first writer approves of the plan, and the second disapproves. One word reveals the writer's attitude.

Example 3: Personification. “The old pickup truck groaned up the hill, complaining about every inch.”

Name it: personification (a truck cannot groan or complain the way a person does). Unpack it: the truck is compared to a tired person struggling up a hill. Effect: you can hear the engine straining, and you understand that the truck is old and barely making it.

Example 4: Tone vs. mood. “Grandma's kitchen always smelled of cinnamon and coffee. I can still see her humming at the stove, flour on her apron, waving me in for one more biscuit.”

Tone (the narrator's attitude): loving and nostalgic, shown by “always,” “I can still see,” and the fond details. Mood (how the reader feels): warm and comforting, created by the smells, the humming, and the invitation for “one more biscuit.”

Try it

1. “Jamal was elated when he passed his test; he called his mother, his brother, and his old coach before he even left the parking lot.” What does elated mean?

Show answer

Extremely happy or thrilled. Clue: he could not wait to call three people with the news.

2. “The classroom was a beehive the morning of the field trip.” Name the figure of speech and explain it.

Show answer

Metaphor (no like or as). The classroom is compared to a beehive: busy, buzzing with noise, and full of activity.

3. “My little brother eats like a vacuum cleaner.” Name the figure of speech and explain it.

Show answer

Simile (uses like). He eats very fast and eats everything in sight.

4. “The apartment was cramped.” Is cramped positive or negative? Give a word with a more positive connotation.

Show answer

Negative. More positive choices: cozy, snug, or compact.

5. “Don't worry about the quiz. It was a piece of cake.” What does the idiom mean?

Show answer

The quiz was very easy. It has nothing to do with real cake.
post:
Summary of key points

  • A word's meaning on the GED is its meaning in context. Use definition, example, contrast, and cause-and-effect clues, then check with the replacement test.
  • Denotation is the dictionary meaning. Connotation is the positive, negative, or neutral feeling a word carries.
  • Tone is the writer's or narrator's attitude. Mood is the feeling the reader gets.
  • A simile compares using like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human qualities to something not human. An idiom is a common expression that does not mean what its words say.
  • For any figure of speech: name it, unpack it, explain the effect.

Exit ticket

1. In one sentence each, define tone and mood.

Show answer

Tone is the writer's or narrator's attitude toward the subject. Mood is the feeling or atmosphere the reader experiences.

2. “The fog was a gray blanket over the harbor.” Simile or metaphor? How do you know?

Show answer

Metaphor. It says the fog was a blanket and does not use like or as.

3. Which word has a more negative connotation, slim or scrawny?

Show answer

Scrawny. It suggests weak and underfed, while slim suggests attractive.

4. “Rosa told a joke to break the ice at the meeting.” What does “break the ice” mean?

Show answer

To ease tension and help people start talking comfortably.

5. What should you do after choosing an answer to a word-in-context question?

Show answer

Put the answer into the sentence in place of the word and reread it to make sure the meaning still works.

Reflection

  • Which was harder for you this week: figuring out word meaning, naming the tone or mood, or explaining figurative language? Why?
  • Think of a song, show, or conversation from this week that used an idiom or a metaphor. What did it really mean?
  • Where in your own life (at work, in texts, in emails) does word choice change how people react to you?

Day 7Finish the Practice GED if needed. Review every missed question and list the skills to work on.30 min

Test-taking strategy: Put it back in the sentence

On any word or phrase question, do not stop when a choice “sounds like” the right definition. Plug your choice into the sentence in place of the original word and reread the whole sentence, plus the one before and after it. If the sentence still makes sense and keeps the same feeling, you have the answer. Test makers often include a choice that is a true meaning of the word but does not fit the passage. The replacement test catches it every time.

vocab.def: A hint in the words or sentences around an unfamiliar word that helps you figure out its meaning.
vocab.example: In “Leo was reticent, unlike his chatty brother,” the contrast with chatty is the clue.

vocab.def: A word with more than one meaning; the sentence tells you which meaning the writer intends.
vocab.example: Modest can mean humble or small: “a modest paycheck” means a small one.

vocab.def: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word.
vocab.example: The denotation of home is the place where someone lives.

vocab.def: The feeling or idea a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning: positive, negative, or neutral.
vocab.example: Home suggests warmth and belonging; residence sounds neutral and formal.

vocab.def: The writer's or narrator's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice and details.
vocab.example: A review that calls a movie “a two-hour nap” has a mocking tone.

vocab.def: The feeling or atmosphere a text creates in the reader.
vocab.example: A story set in a dark, silent house at midnight may have an eerie mood.

vocab.def: Words that mean exactly what they say.
Words used in an imaginative way to mean more than, or something different from, their literal meaning.
A comparison of two unlike things using like or as.
vocab.example: The baby's hands were as soft as flour.

vocab.def: A comparison that says one thing is another, without using like or as.
vocab.example: Her laugh was music to the tired crew.

vocab.def: Giving human actions, feelings, or qualities to an animal, object, or idea.
vocab.example: The old floorboards complained under every step.

vocab.def: A common expression whose meaning cannot be figured out from the meanings of its individual words.
vocab.example: “Hit the books” means to study hard.

vocab.def: Extreme exaggeration used for emphasis or humor, not meant to be taken literally.
Descriptive language that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch).
vocab.example: The sizzle of onions and the smell of fresh bread filled the kitchen.

vocab.def: The specific words a writer selects to create meaning, tone, and mood (also called diction).

notes:
Week 4 RLA Study Sheet: Word Meaning, Tone, and Figurative Language

Context clues

  • Definition: the sentence explains the word
  • Example: such as, including, for example
  • Contrast: but, although, unlike, however
  • Cause/effect: so, because, as a result

Replacement test: put the choice in place of the word and reread. It must make sense in this sentence.

Connotation

Denotation = dictionary meaning. Connotation = feeling (+, −, neutral).

thrifty (+) / cheap (−)   curious (+) / nosy (−)   determined (+) / stubborn (−)

Tone vs. mood

  • Tone: writer's attitude (amused, bitter, admiring, nostalgic)
  • Mood: reader's feeling (tense, gloomy, peaceful, hopeful)

Highlight strong words → sort + or − → pick a precise word. Avoid extremes.

Figure of speech: 3 steps

  1. Name it.
  2. Unpack it: what is compared to what?
  3. Explain the effect: what do I see or feel?
TypeSignalExample
Similelike or asquiet as a library
Metaphorone thing is anotherThe hallway was a tomb.
Personificationhuman action or feeling for a non-human thingThe furnace groaned.
Idiomwords do not add up to the meaningon the fence = undecided
Hyperbolebig exaggerationa million times

Common mistakes: picking the dictionary meaning instead of the context meaning; mixing up tone and mood; reading idioms literally; calling every comparison a metaphor; choosing extreme tone words.

stimuli.title: Last Call at the Blue Kettle
stimuli.html:
[1] The bell over the door of the Blue Kettle had rung for thirty-one years, and tonight Marisol Ortega wanted to hear it one more time. She stood behind the counter with a rag in her hand, wiping a spot that was already clean. Outside, the rain came down in gray sheets, and the parking lot was as empty as a church on a Monday.

[2] The diner had been her husband's dream before it was hers. Ernesto had bought it with a bank loan, a borrowed truck, and more nerve than sense. “You two will be eating beans until you're fifty,” her sister had warned. Ernesto only laughed. He painted the walls the color of butter and hung a sign in the window that promised COFFEE HOT AS GOSSIP. For years the place hummed. Truckers, nurses coming off the night shift, teenagers splitting a single plate of fries four ways: they all found their way to the Blue Kettle. The long counter was the town's front porch, and Ernesto knew every one of their orders by heart.

[3] Now a highway bypass had opened two miles east, and the traffic had dried up like a creek in August. Ernesto had been gone for three years. The landlord had been polite but firm. Marisol had signed the papers on Tuesday. Tomorrow a crew would come for the grill.

[4] She turned off the neon sign in the window. Without its pink glow, the room looked smaller and older. The stools stood in a crooked line like old men waiting for a bus that would never come. The coffee maker sighed as it cooled. Somewhere in the back, the ice machine dropped one last batch of cubes with a sound like scattered applause.

[5] Marisol thought about the night of the big ice storm, when the power went out across the county and half the town crowded into the diner because Ernesto had a gas stove and a stubborn streak. He had cooked by candlelight until dawn. People still stopped her at the grocery store to talk about that night. “Your husband kept us all afloat,” one woman told her once, squeezing her hand. Marisol had not trusted her voice to answer.

[6] The bell rang.

[7] She looked up, ready to say they were closed. In the doorway stood Danny Pruitt, rain dripping from the brim of his cap. He had been one of those teenagers splitting fries. Now he had gray in his beard and a boy of about ten beside him.

[8] “Heard tonight was the last night,” Danny said. “I wanted him to see it. Before.”

[9] Marisol looked at the boy, who was staring at the pie case as if it held treasure. Then she looked at the cold grill, the stacked chairs, the mop bucket by the door. She had planned to be finished by now. She had planned to go home, sit in the quiet, and let it be over.

[10] She reached up and switched the neon sign back on.

[11] “Sit anywhere,” she said. “The coffee's still hot.”
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: The Deep End
stimuli.html:
[1] I learned to swim the year I turned thirty-eight, which is a little like learning to ride a bike the year you get your driver's license. For most of my life, I had treated water the way some people treat dogs that bark behind fences: I kept my distance and pretended I was not afraid.

[2] My excuse had always been practical. I grew up in a town where the only pool belonged to a motel, and the motel did not welcome kids from my street. By the time I was an adult, not swimming had hardened into part of who I was, like a crooked tooth I had stopped noticing. Then my daughter, Keisha, joined a swim team, and I found myself sitting in the bleachers every Saturday, cheering for something I could not do.

[3] The adult beginner class met at 6 a.m. at the community pool on Fulton Street. There were five of us: a retired mail carrier, two college students, a man who drove a forklift, and me. Our instructor, Ms. Abernathy, was about five feet tall and had a voice that could cut through a thunderstorm. On the first morning, she told us to put our faces in the water and blow bubbles. I felt ridiculous. I also could not do it. Every time my nose touched the surface, my whole body staged a protest.

[4] “Your body is not your enemy,” Ms. Abernathy said. “It's just a nervous employee. Give it clear instructions.”

[5] So I gave it instructions. Breathe in. Face down. Breathe out slowly. Week by week, the water stopped feeling like a wall and started feeling like a place. By the fifth week, I could float on my back, staring up at the water-stained ceiling tiles, my ears full of the pool's low hum. By the eighth, I could swim one awkward, splashing length of the pool. It was not pretty. The forklift driver said I swam like a shopping cart with a bad wheel, and he was not wrong.

[6] The last class ended with a test: swim across the deep end, where the floor drops to twelve feet. I stood at the edge with my toes curled over the tile. My heart was pounding so hard I was sure the others could hear it. Then I looked at Keisha, who had insisted on coming that morning and was sitting in the bleachers, and I jumped.

[7] I would love to report that I glided across like a dolphin. I did not. I thrashed, I swallowed half the pool, and I reached the far wall in what Ms. Abernathy generously called “a time.” But I reached it. When I looked up, my daughter was on her feet, shouting my name as if I had just won a gold medal.

[8] I still swim on Saturdays. I am still slow. But the water and I have reached an understanding, and that is more than I ever expected.
stimuli.source: Original personal narrative written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Draft Article: Volunteer Spotlight
stimuli.html:
Volunteer Spotlight: Gloria Haines
(Draft article for the Grace Street Community Center newsletter)

(1) This month's Volunteer Spotlight shines on Gloria Haines, who has run the Saturday food pantry at the Grace Street Community Center for six years. (2) Every week, Gloria arrives at 7 a.m. to unload the delivery truck, sort donations, and set up tables before the doors open. (3) Families who visit the pantry say Gloria is (A); she remembers their children's names and always asks how they are doing.

(4) Gloria's dedication is clearest in a crisis. (5) When the pantry's only freezer broke down last July, Gloria (B) and raised $1,200 from neighbors and local businesses in a single weekend. (6) Not one pound of donated food was lost.

(7) Ask anyone at the center, and they will tell you the same thing: Gloria is (C). (8) Volunteers who would like to work alongside her can sign up at the front desk.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the narrator says that Ernesto “knew every one of their orders by heart.” What does this phrase mean?
options: He had memorized what each regular customer usually ordered.
He cared deeply about his customers' feelings.
He wrote down every order carefully before cooking it.
He served only the foods that he loved most.
items.hint: “By heart” is an idiom. It has nothing to do with the heart as an organ or with feelings.
items.explain:
Step 1. Recognize the idiom. Read literally, “knew by heart” does not make sense, so it is a common expression with its own meaning.

Step 2. “To know something by heart” means to have it memorized. Check the context: the same customers (truckers, nurses, teenagers) came again and again, so Ernesto would have learned their usual orders.

Step 3. Replacement test: “Ernesto had memorized every one of their orders.” It fits. Correct answer: He had memorized what each regular customer usually ordered.

Why not the others? “Cared deeply about his customers' feelings” reads the word heart literally, which is the main trap. Nothing in the passage says he wrote orders down or served only his favorite foods.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the author writes that the parking lot was “as empty as a church on a Monday.” This phrase is an example of—
options: a simile
a metaphor
personification
an idiom
items.hint: Look for the signal word that comes before “a church.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the two things being compared: the parking lot and a church on a Monday (when most churches are empty).

Step 2. Look for the signal word. The comparison uses as (“as empty as”). A comparison of two unlike things using like or as is a simile. Correct.

Step 3. Rule out the others. A metaphor would say the lot was a church, with no like or as. Personification would give the lot a human action, which does not happen here. An idiom is a fixed common saying; this is a fresh comparison the author created.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 4 that uses personification: it describes an object doing something only a person can do, without making a comparison using like or as.
spans: She turned off the neon sign in the window.
Without its pink glow, the room looked smaller and older.
The stools stood in a crooked line like old men waiting for a bus that would never come.
The coffee maker sighed as it cooled.
Somewhere in the back, the ice machine dropped one last batch of cubes with a sound like scattered applause.
items.hint: Which object is described with an action that people do when they are tired or sad?
items.explain:
Step 1. Personification gives a human action or feeling to something that is not human.

Step 2. Check each sentence. In “The coffee maker sighed as it cooled,” a machine sighs, which is something a tired or sad person does. There is no like or as comparison. Correct. (The word as here means “while,” not a comparison.)

Step 3. Rule out the others. Sentence 1 is literal: Marisol really turns off the sign. Sentence 2 is literal description. Sentences 3 and 5 use like to compare (stools to old men, the sound of ice to applause), so they are similes.

Effect: the sighing coffee maker makes even the machines seem tired and sad, adding to the feeling that the diner is ending.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the narrator says Ernesto bought the diner with “more nerve than sense.” What does this phrase suggest about Ernesto?
options: He was bold enough to take a big risk, even though the plan was not very cautious.
He was a nervous man who was easily upset by problems.
He knew very little about cooking when he bought the diner.
He was dishonest with the bank about how much money he had.
items.hint: Here, nerve means courage, and sense means good judgment. Also look at how his sister reacts.
items.explain:
Step 1. Determine the meaning of each key word in context. Here, nerve means courage or daring (as in “it took nerve to do that”), not nervousness. Sense means careful, practical judgment.

Step 2. Put it together: he had more courage than caution. The context supports this: he used a loan and a borrowed truck, his sister warned they would be “eating beans until you're fifty,” and he “only laughed.”

Step 3. The phrase has a fond, slightly teasing connotation: the risk was not sensible, but it was brave. Correct answer: He was bold enough to take a big risk, even though the plan was not very cautious.

Why not the others? “Nervous” is the main trap: it confuses nerve (courage) with nervous (anxious). The passage says nothing about his cooking skill or about lying to the bank.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the author writes that “the traffic had dried up like a creek in August.” What does this comparison suggest?
options: The number of cars passing the diner had gradually shrunk to almost nothing.
The road in front of the diner flooded every summer.
The diner lost customers only during the summer months.
Drivers stopped coming because the weather had become too hot.
items.hint: Picture what happens to a small stream during the hottest, driest month. Then apply that to traffic.
items.explain:
Step 1. Name it: a simile (it uses like). Traffic is compared to a creek in August.

Step 2. Unpack it: in the heat of late summer, a creek slowly loses water until little or none is left. The shared quality is a steady flow that shrinks and disappears.

Step 3. Apply it to the context: the bypass opened two miles away, so the cars that once flowed past the diner now go elsewhere. Correct answer: The number of cars passing the diner had gradually shrunk to almost nothing.

Why not the others? These choices take the comparison literally. The simile is not about real water, weather, or the month of August; the passage says the cause was the new bypass.

items.prompt: Drag each phrase from the story into the category that names the type of figurative language it uses.
choices: “as empty as a church on a Monday”
“The long counter was the town's front porch”
“The coffee maker sighed as it cooled”
“knew every one of their orders by heart”
items.hint: Check for like or as first. Then ask: does it say one thing is another? Does an object act like a person? Is it a common saying?
items.explain:
“as empty as a church on a Monday” → Simile. It compares the parking lot to a church using as.

“The long counter was the town's front porch” → Metaphor. It says the counter was a front porch, with no like or as. It suggests a friendly gathering place where neighbors sat and talked.

“The coffee maker sighed as it cooled” → Personification. A machine is given a human action (sighing). The word as here means “while,” so it is not a simile.

“knew every one of their orders by heart” → Idiom. “By heart” is a common expression meaning “from memory.”

“with a sound like scattered applause” → Simile. It compares the sound of falling ice to clapping using like.

Common error: placing the coffee maker in Simile because of the word as. Always check whether as is actually making a comparison.

items.prompt: Which phrase best describes the mood the author creates in paragraph 4?
options: lonely and sorrowful
tense and frightening
joyful and lively
angry and bitter
items.hint: Highlight the descriptive details in paragraph 4. Are they mostly about energy, danger, or emptiness?
items.explain:
Step 1. Highlight the strongest details: the glow disappears and the room looks “smaller and older”; the stools are “like old men waiting for a bus that would never come”; the coffee maker “sighed”; the ice machine drops its “one last batch.”

Step 2. Sort them. These details describe emptiness, age, waiting with no hope, and endings. They make the reader feel sad and alone with Marisol.

Step 3. Choose the precise words: lonely and sorrowful. Correct.

Why not the others? “Tense and frightening” is the most tempting wrong answer because it is night and raining, but nothing in the paragraph is threatening or dangerous. “Applause” might suggest joy, but it is only a comparison for the sound of ice in an empty room, so “joyful and lively” does not fit. Nothing shows anger or bitterness.

items.prompt: In paragraph 10, Marisol switches the neon sign back on. How does this action affect the mood at the end of the story?
options: It shifts the mood from sad finality to warmth and hope, as the diner brings people together one last time.
It creates suspense about whether Danny will be able to pay for the meal.
It shows that Marisol has decided to keep the diner open for good.
It reveals Marisol's anger that customers stayed away until the very last night.
items.hint: Compare what the sign being turned off meant in paragraph 4 with what turning it back on means now.
items.explain:
Step 1. Recall what the sign stood for earlier. In paragraph 4, turning it off made the room look “smaller and older” and began the sad, empty mood of closing for good.

Step 2. Look at what changes. Danny, a former teenage customer, arrives with his son to see the diner “before” it closes. Marisol had planned to go home and “let it be over,” but she switches the sign back on and says, “Sit anywhere. The coffee's still hot.”

Step 3. Name the effect. The light returns, and so does the diner's purpose as a gathering place. The mood shifts from loss to warmth and hope. Correct answer: It shifts the mood from sad finality to warmth and hope, as the diner brings people together one last time.

Why not the others? “Keep the diner open for good” is the main trap: it goes beyond the text. She has already signed the papers, and a crew is coming for the grill tomorrow. Nothing suggests suspense about payment or anger toward customers; her words are welcoming.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the author writes that “not swimming had hardened into part of who I was.” As used in this sentence, hardened most nearly means—
options: become fixed and difficult to change
grown physically stiff and sore
become cruel and unfeeling
frozen into solid ice
items.hint: Read the comparison that follows in the same sentence: “like a crooked tooth I had stopped noticing.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the whole sentence and the one before it. As a child she had no chance to learn. By the time she was an adult, not swimming had “hardened into part of who I was, like a crooked tooth I had stopped noticing.”

Step 2. Use the clue. A crooked tooth is a permanent part of you that you stop thinking about. So hardened describes a habit that became set and permanent over time.

Step 3. Replacement test: “not swimming had become fixed as part of who I was.” It makes sense. Correct answer: become fixed and difficult to change.

Why not the others? “Become cruel and unfeeling” is a real meaning of hardened (as in “a hardened heart”), but it describes people's feelings, and the author is not describing cruelty. “Physically stiff” and “frozen into ice” are literal meanings that do not fit a habit.

items.prompt: The author often pokes fun at herself in this narrative. Which two details most clearly create this humorous, self-mocking tone? Select two answers.
options: “The forklift driver said I swam like a shopping cart with a bad wheel, and he was not wrong.”
“I thrashed, I swallowed half the pool, and I reached the far wall”
“The adult beginner class met at 6 a.m. at the community pool on Fulton Street.”
“my daughter was on her feet, shouting my name as if I had just won a gold medal”
“I grew up in a town where the only pool belonged to a motel”
items.hint: Self-mocking humor makes fun of the writer herself. Which details exaggerate or laugh at how badly she swam?
items.explain:
Step 1. Define the target. A self-mocking tone means the writer jokes about her own weaknesses.

Step 2. Test each option. Shopping cart with a bad wheel: a funny simile for her clumsy, lopsided swimming, and she agrees (“he was not wrong”). Self-mocking. Correct. Swallowed half the pool: a hyperbole (obvious exaggeration) that laughs at her messy swim. Self-mocking. Correct.

Step 3. Rule out the rest. The 6 a.m. class detail is plain, factual information. The motel pool detail explains a real barrier from her childhood and is serious, not joking. The daughter “shouting my name as if I had just won a gold medal” is the strongest distractor: it is a comparison, but it expresses the daughter's pride and the warmth of the moment. It does not make fun of the author.

items.prompt: In paragraph 7, the author says she reached the far wall “in what Ms. Abernathy generously called ‘a time.’” Why does the author most likely use the word generously?
options: to suggest that her swim was so slow that even calling it “a time” was a kindness
to show that Ms. Abernathy gave her extra minutes because she was the oldest student
to suggest that Ms. Abernathy was proud because the author had the fastest time in the class
to show that Ms. Abernathy was impatient and annoyed with the author's slow progress
items.hint: Read the sentences just before the phrase. How well did the swim go? Then ask what it means to describe something “generously.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Consider the context. Just before, the author says she did not glide “like a dolphin”; she “thrashed” and “swallowed half the pool.” The swim was slow and messy.

Step 2. Consider the connotation. To describe something generously is to describe it more kindly than it deserves. The quotation marks around “a time” add to the joke: her swim was so slow it barely counted as a time at all.

Step 3. Connect to tone. The word continues the author's gentle, self-mocking humor, and it shows that the instructor was kind. Correct answer: to suggest that her swim was so slow that even calling it “a time” was a kindness.

Why not the others? “Gave her extra minutes” reads generously as literally giving something away, and nothing says she was the oldest or got extra time. “Fastest time” contradicts the passage. “Impatient and annoyed” is the opposite of the word's positive connotation.

items.skill: Word choice: connotation, idioms, and tone
items.prompt:
Read the draft newsletter article. The article is meant to honor Gloria in a warm, respectful way. Choose the option that best completes each blank so that the word choice fits both the meaning and the tone of the article.

Sentence 3, blank (A): Families who visit the pantry say Gloria is {{0}}; she remembers their children's names and always asks how they are doing.

Sentence 5, blank (B): When the pantry's only freezer broke down last July, Gloria {{1}} and raised $1,200 from neighbors and local businesses in a single weekend.

Sentence 7, blank (C): Ask anyone at the center, and they will tell you the same thing: Gloria is {{2}}.

options: caring
nosy
pushy
prying
jumped into action
jumped the gun
jumped ship
jumped on the bandwagon
the heart of the pantry
an adequate volunteer, more or less
kind of a big deal, I guess
the loudest person in the pantry

items.hint: For (A) and (C), choose the words with a positive connotation that suit a formal tribute. For (B), think about what each idiom really means: which one describes acting quickly to solve a problem?
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The detail after the semicolon (she remembers children's names and asks how families are doing) describes kindness. Step 2: All four words could describe someone who asks questions, but they differ in connotation. Nosy, pushy, and prying are negative; they suggest she is intruding. Step 3: The article honors Gloria, so the positive word fits: caring. Correct.

Blank (B). Step 1: The sentence describes a problem (the freezer broke) and a fast solution ($1,200 raised in one weekend, so no food was lost). Step 2: Test each idiom. “Jumped into action” means acted quickly and energetically. Correct. “Jumped the gun” means acted too soon, before the right time. “Jumped ship” means abandoned a group or job, the opposite of what she did. “Jumped on the bandwagon” means joined something only because it was popular.

Blank (C). Step 1: The article's tone is warm and respectful. Step 2: “The heart of the pantry” is a metaphor: like a heart keeping a body alive, Gloria keeps the pantry running. It is positive and fits a tribute. Correct. “An adequate volunteer, more or less” is faint praise and sounds unkind. “Kind of a big deal, I guess” is too casual and sounds unsure. “The loudest person in the pantry” has a negative or teasing connotation and does not match the article's purpose.
